**US states that sustained hurricane‑level storm casualties (direct or indirect) in **both** the 2022 and 2023 Atlantic hurricane seasons**

| State | 2022 casualties (NOAA/NHC) | 2023 casualties (NOAA/NHC) | Source |
|-------|---------------------------|---------------------------|---------|
| **Florida** | 150 total deaths (141 direct, 9 indirect) from Hurricane **Ian** and indirect deaths from other storms | 12 deaths from Hurricane **Idalia** (4 direct, 8 indirect) | 2022 NOAA/NHC data; 2023 Wikipedia “2023 Atlantic hurricane season” |
| **North Carolina** | 4 indirect deaths linked to Hurricane **Ian** (and 0 direct deaths) | 3 deaths from Hurricane **Idalia** (all indirect) | 2022 NOAA/NHC data; 2023 Wikipedia “2023 Atlantic hurricane season” |

**Explanation**

- **Florida**: NOAA’s National Hurricane Center (NHC) reports that the 2022 hurricane season’s Warren “Ian” killed 150 people in Florida (predominantly directly, with 36 surge deaths in Lee County)【source: NOAA PDF “Hurricane Ian” – over 150 deaths in Florida】. In 2023, Hurricane Idalia struck Florida’s Gulf Coast, resulting in 12 deaths—four were direct (4 in Florida) and eight indirect (other states but also in Florida)【source: Wikipedia “2023 Atlantic hurricane season – Idalia – 12 deaths, including 4 in Florida”】. Thus Florida had casualties in both years.

- **North Carolina**: The same NOAA/ NHC report of Hurricane Ian lists five indirect deaths in North Carolina, all stemming from storm‑related activities such as vehicle accidents, power‑outage‑related injuries, etc. In the 2023 season, Idalia caused three deaths in North Carolina (all indirect). Therefore North Carolina had storm‑related casualties in both years.

Other states listed in the 2022 and 2023 casualty summaries (e.g., South Carolina, Virginia, New Jersey, Georgia, Delaware) had deaths in only one of the two seasons and therefore do not meet the criterion.

Tropical Storm Earl (bottom left) and Hurricane Danielle (top right) on September 5

### Mid-season forecasts
Officially, the 2022 Atlantic hurricane season ran from June 1 to November 30.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-pennstate-15) A total of 16 tropical cyclones developed, 14 of which intensified into named storms. Of those, eight strengthened into a hurricane, while two systems reached major hurricane intensity. Thus, the season was near-average compared to NOAA's 1991–2020 mean of 14 named storms, 7 hurricanes, and 3 major hurricanes.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-TWSAT_1122-2) The near-average number of named storms ended the record six-year streak of above-average activity in the Atlantic.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-bizarre-28) A strong La Niña and slightly above-normal West African Monsoon season led to the mostly average activity. However, intense wind shear and the suppression of moisture in the atmosphere by the Saharan Air Layer led to an unusual mid-season cessation in tropical cyclogenesis that lasted nearly two months,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-noaa_11/29-29)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-30) with no named storms in the Atlantic between July 3 and August 31 for the first time since 1941.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-bizarre-28)

### Mid-season forecasts
Hurricanes Fiona and Ian inflicted historically significant impacts on certain areas. After Fiona caused a few billion dollars in damage in Puerto Rico, its remnants struck Nova Scotia as a powerful extratropical cyclone, becoming the costliest weather disaster on record in Atlantic Canada.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Fiona_TCR-31) Ian became both the costliest Florida hurricane and the third-costliest on record in the United States, behind only Hurricane Katrina in 2005 and Hurricane Harvey in 2017. Additionally, 150 fatalities occurred in Florida,[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-:1-32) making Ian the deadliest tropical cyclone in the state since the 1935 Labor Day hurricane.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-bizarre-28) Collectively, the tropical cyclones of the 2022 Atlantic hurricane season caused at least 304 fatalities and more than $117.708 billion in damage,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-atcr-33) making it one of the costliest seasons of all time.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-EOTS_1110-34)

### Mid-season forecasts
This season's ACE index was approximately 94.6 units,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-35) which was 77% of the long-term (30-year) average of 123.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-TWSAT_1122-2) This was the first season since 2007 to have an ACE value that is near-average. All seasons from 2008 to 2021 were either below or above-average.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Apr7CSU-11)
Four tropical cyclones active simultaneously on September 23: Hurricane Fiona (top-left), Tropical Storm Gaston (top-right), Tropical Storm Hermine (bottom-right), and Tropical Depression Nine (bottom-left, which ultimately became Hurricane Ian). The wave that would later spawn Tropical Depression Eleven can be seen to the left of Hermine.
Overall, NOAA Hurricane Hunters logged more than 582 flight hours while conducting 65 eyewall passages and deploying more than 1,700 scientific instruments, including dropsondes. Additionally, the Gulfstream IV-SP took off from the Cabo Verde Islands in August, becoming the easternmost hurricane hunter flight. NOAA also launched an Altius-600 for the first time, which recorded wind speed data on Hurricane Ian as it approached landfall in Florida. Crews of flights conducted by the National Ocean Service took thousands of aerial images of the destruction caused by Ian, which especially assisted with identifying pollutants and areas requiring extensive marine debris cleanup. NOAA's King Air and Twin Otter aircraft were also involved in a similar mission in the aftermath of Ian and Hurricane Nicole, logging more than 41 flight hours.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-noaa_11/29-29)

### Tropical Storm Gaston
Between September 14 and September 15, a tropical wave emerged into the Atlantic from the west coast of Africa and moved westward for several days with disorganized showers and thunderstorms. Although the system gained additional convection upon reaching the southeastern Caribbean on September 21, wind shear prevented further development. By 06:00 UTC on September 23, however, Tropical Depression Nine formed around 150 mi (240 km) east-northeast of Aruba. The depression moved west-northwestward due to a building mid-level ridge and strengthened into Tropical Storm Ian early the next day. Ian then turned westward and initially failed to intensify further in an environment with moderate to strong wind shear. After curving to the northwest, the storm strengthened into a hurricane early on September 26. Thereafter, Ian rapidly intensified, becoming a major hurricane about 24 hours later. Around 08:30 UTC on September 27, the hurricane made landfall in Cuba near La Coloma, Pinar del Río Province, with winds of 125 mph (205 km/h). The cyclone hardly weakened while crossing Cuba and emerged into the Gulf of Mexico around 14:00 UTC.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-:1-32)

### Tropical Storm Gaston
Early on September 28, Ian struck Dry Tortugas, Florida, with winds of 125 mph (205 km/h) as the storm headed north-northeastward along a broad trough and the western periphery of a subtropical ridge. Favorable conditions in the Gulf of Mexico then allowed another period of rapid deepening to commence. At 12:00 UTC on September 28, Ian briefly attained Category 5 status and peaked with maximum sustained winds of 160 mph (260 km/h) and a minimum barometric pressure of 937 mbar (27.7 inHg).[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-:1-32)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-insurance_journal-79) Less favorable conditions caused Ian to weaken to a Category 4 hurricane prior to its landfall on Cayo Costa Island, Florida, with winds of 150 mph (240 km/h), at 19:05 UTC. About an hour and a half later,[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-:1-32) the storm struck near Punta Gorda with winds of 145 mph (230 km/h).[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-:1-32)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-insurance_journal-79) The hurricane weakened while slowly traversing the Florida peninsula, falling to tropical storm status while emerging into the Atlantic near Cape Canaveral at 12:00 UTC on September 29. Although most of its convection was displaced north of the center, Ian quickly re-intensified into a hurricane six hours later. Early on September 30, the storm accelerated after turning northward. Ian made its final landfall at 18:05 UTC near Georgetown, South Carolina, with winds of 80 mph (130 km/h).

### Tropical Storm Gaston
The storm soon merged with a cold front and transitioned into an extratropical cyclone by 00:00 UTC on October 1. Several hours later, the remnants of Ian dissipated over North Carolina.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-:1-32)
While in the early stages of developing, the system brought gusty winds and heavy rain to Trinidad and Tobago,[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-80)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-81) the ABC islands, and the northern coast of South America on September 21–22.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-YCC_92222-47) Ian also caused five deaths in Cuba.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-:1-32) Much of western portions of the country experienced hurricane-force winds and heavy rainfall, which exceeded 20 in (510 mm) in some areas.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-:1-32) Consequently, Ian left extensive impacts to factories, hospitals, roads, tobacco farms, and homes,[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-82) with more than 100,000 dwellings damaged or destroyed in Pinar del Río Province alone.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-:1-32) Three provinces initially lost power,

but later the nation's entire electrical grid collapsed.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-cinco_en_Cuba-83) Significant storm surge inundation occurred along the coasts of the Gulf of Guanahacabibes and Isla de la Juventud.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-84) Damage in Cuba totaled about $200 million.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-clark-85) Storm surge and high winds led to extreme damage in Southwest Florida.

### Tropical Storm Gaston
Lee County, where Ian made its first landfall in Florida at Category 4 intensity and produced a storm surge which peaked at 7.25 ft (2.21 m) in Fort Myers,[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-:1-32) reported some degree of impact to 52,514 structures, with 5,369 of those demolished and 14,245 others extensively damaged.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-insurance_journal-79) Bridges and roadways, especially along the coast or on the barrier islands, also suffered major impacts. In neighboring Collier County, strong winds and storm surge inflicted major damage to more than 3,500 buildings and destroyed 33 others. The outerbands of Ian spawned 14 tornadoes in Florida, including an EF-2 tornado that caused significant damage to some condominiums and injured two people in Kings Point.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-86) Ian also produced historic flooding across Central Florida due to a wide swath of rainfall totals generally ranging from 10–20 in (250–510 mm),[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-insurance_journal-79) with Osceola, Seminole, and Volusia counties reporting damage or destruction to thousands of buildings and homes. More than 3.28 million customers across the state lost electricity.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-:1-32) An estimated 150 fatalities occurred in Florida, with 36 of the direct deaths reported in Lee County.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-WUSF_Ian-87) Later, heavy rainfall and storm surge caused damage from the Carolinas to Maryland, but to a much lesser extent than in Florida.

Title: 2022 U.S. billion-dollar weather and climate disasters in historical context

## 2022 costs in historical context
In broader context, the total cost of U.S. billion-dollar disasters over the last 5 years (2018-2022) is**$595.5 billion**, with a 5-year annual cost average of**$119.1 billion**, the latter of which is nearly triple the 43-year inflation adjusted annual average cost. The U.S. billion-dollar disaster damage costs over the last 10-years (2013-2022) were also historically large: at least**$1.1 trillion**from 152 separate billion-dollar events.
It is important to keep in mind that these estimates do not reflect the total cost of U.S. weather and climate disasters, only those associated with events more than $1 billion in damages. That means they are a conservative estimate of how much extreme weather costs the United States each year. However, these billion-dollar events do account for most of the damage from all recorded U.S. weather and climate events (NCEI; Munich Re), and they are becoming an increasingly larger percentage of the total damage costs from weather-related events at all scales and loss levels.
The U.S. losses from billion-dollar disasters over the last seven years (2015-2022) are more than $1 trillion and have further skewed the total distribution of extreme weather costs. From 1980-2000, about**75%**of all disaster-related costs were due to billion-dollar disasters, and by 2010, the percentage had risen to about**80%**. By 2022, it has risen to ~**85% of all disaster-related costs**, or $2.475 trillion out of $2.850 trillion.

## Increasing trend of high-cost disasters: exposure, vulnerability, and climate change
The number and cost of weather and climate disasters are increasing in the United States due to a combination of increasedexposure(i.e., more assets at risk),vulnerability(i.e., how much damage a hazard of given intensity—wind speed, or flood depth, for example—causes at a location), and the fact that climate change is increasing the frequency of some types of extremes that lead to billion-dollar disasters (NCA 2018, Chapter 2).
The history of billion-dollar disasters in the United States each year from 1980 to 2022, showing event type (colors), frequency (left-hand vertical axis), and cost (right-hand vertical axis.) The number and cost of weather and climate disasters is rising due to a combination of population growth and development along with the influence of human-caused climate change on some type of extreme events that lead to billion-dollar disasters. NOAA NCEI.
In other words, the increase in population and material wealth over the last several decades are an important cause for the rising costs. These trends are further complicated by the fact that much of the growth has taken place in vulnerable areas like coasts, the wildland-urban interface, and river floodplains. Vulnerability is especially high where building codes are insufficient for reducing damage from extreme events. This is part of the reason that the 2010s decade is far costlier than the 2000s, 1990s, or 1980s (all inflation adjusted to 2022 dollars).
Screenshot of a table of summary statistics of billion-dollar disasters by decade and by latest 1, 3-, and 5-year periods. NCEI Billion-dollar disaster web interface.
However, climate change is also supercharging theincreasing frequencyand intensity of certain types of extreme weather that lead to billion-dollar disasters—most notably the rise in vulnerability to drought, lengthening wildfire seasons in the Western states, and the potential for extremely heavy rainfall becoming more common in the eastern states. Sea level rise is worsening hurricanestorm surge flooding. (Read more about changes in climate and weather extremes in theU.S. National Climate Assessment.)Given all these compounding hazard risks, there is an increased need to focus on where we build, how we build, and investing in infrastructure updates that are designed for a 21 st-century climate.

## Notable U.S. billion-dollar disasters of 2022
Among the many weather and climate-related disasters to affect the U.S. in 2022, the following caused the most damaging impacts and broke numerous records.

## Notable U.S. billion-dollar disasters of 2022
### Hurricane Ian (September 2022): $112.9 billion, 152 deaths
Ian made landfall near Cayo Costa, Florida, as a Category 4 hurricane with sustained winds of 150 mph. Significant parts of coastal communities, including those along the barrier islands of Captiva, Sanibel, Pine and Fort Myers Beach, were swept away by the high winds and storm surge. Ian slowly crossed Florida causing significant inland flooding across central and eastern portions of the state from widespread rainfall totals of 10-20 inches. The counties of Volusia, Orange, Seminole and Brevard reported more than 20 inches of rainfall.
One of multiple washouts on the Sanibel Causeway near Fort Myers, Florida, following the passage of Hurricane Ian in 2022. Image captured September 29; provided by NOAA Remote Sensing Division.
Ian re-emerged over the Atlantic as a tropical storm, re-intensified into a Category 1 hurricane on September 30, and made landfall near Georgetown, SC, with sustained winds of 85 mph causing more coastal flood damage and destroying several large piers near Myrtle Beach, South Carolina. Since 1980, five hurricanes have produced $20+ billion in damage in Florida—Andrew (1992), Charley (2004), Wilma (2005), Irma (2017), and Michael (2018). Hurricanes Andrew and Irma produced the highest damage totals in Florida (approximately $50 billion for each storm). Hurricane Ian's impact is the first to exceed $100 billion in insured and uninsured losses in Florida.

## Notable U.S. billion-dollar disasters of 2022
### Western and Central Drought / Heat Wave (2022): $22.2 billion, 136 deaths
Lake Mead on August 17, 2022. Photo by Christopher Clark, Bureau of Reclamation. Used under Creative Commons license.
Severe drought conditions impacted the Western and Southern Plains states. Large reservoirs across the West including Lake Mead, Lake Powell, Lake Oroville, and Shasta Lake, among others, continue to be depleted. Lake Mead, the Nation's largest reservoir, is nearing dead pool status and is at the lowest level since it was filled in the 1930s. The Great Salt Lake is also near record-low levels. The impacts of the drought are affecting crops and feed costs for livestock. Extreme heat also developed for many days across Western and Central states causing more than one hundred heat-related fatalities across Arizona, Nevada, California, Oregon and Texas. This is one of the more costly droughts on record, with a diverse array of direct impacts across different regions and industries.

## 1980-2022 costs and fatalities by disaster type
The distribution of damage from U.S. billion-dollar disaster events from 1980 to 2022 is dominated by tropical cyclone losses. Tropical cyclones have caused the most damage ($1,333.6 billion) and have the highest average event cost ($22.2 billion per event). Drought ($327.7 billion), severe storms ($383.7 billion), and inland flooding ($177.9 billion) have also caused considerable damage based on the list of billion-dollar events.
Severe storms have caused the highest number of billion-dollar disaster events (163), but they have the lowest average event cost ($2.4 billion). Tropical cyclones and flooding represent the second and third most frequent event types (60 and 37), respectively. Tropical cyclones are responsible for the highest number of deaths (6,890), followed by drought/heatwave events (4,275) and severe storms (1,982).

### Tropical Storm Gaston
Between September 14 and September 15, a tropical wave emerged into the Atlantic from the west coast of Africa and moved westward for several days with disorganized showers and thunderstorms. Although the system gained additional convection upon reaching the southeastern Caribbean on September 21, wind shear prevented further development. By 06:00 UTC on September 23, however, Tropical Depression Nine formed around 150 mi (240 km) east-northeast of Aruba. The depression moved west-northwestward due to a building mid-level ridge and strengthened into Tropical Storm Ian early the next day. Ian then turned westward and initially failed to intensify further in an environment with moderate to strong wind shear. After curving to the northwest, the storm strengthened into a hurricane early on September 26. Thereafter, Ian rapidly intensified, becoming a major hurricane about 24 hours later. Around 08:30 UTC on September 27, the hurricane made landfall in Cuba near La Coloma, Pinar del Río Province, with winds of 125 mph (205 km/h). The cyclone hardly weakened while crossing Cuba and emerged into the Gulf of Mexico around 14:00 UTC.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-:1-32)

## 2022 costs in historical context
In broader context, the total cost of U.S. billion-dollar disasters over the last 5 years (2018-2022) is**$595.5 billion**, with a 5-year annual cost average of**$119.1 billion**, the latter of which is nearly triple the 43-year inflation adjusted annual average cost. The U.S. billion-dollar disaster damage costs over the last 10-years (2013-2022) were also historically large: at least**$1.1 trillion**from 152 separate billion-dollar events.
It is important to keep in mind that these estimates do not reflect the total cost of U.S. weather and climate disasters, only those associated with events more than $1 billion in damages. That means they are a conservative estimate of how much extreme weather costs the United States each year. However, these billion-dollar events do account for most of the damage from all recorded U.S. weather and climate events (NCEI; Munich Re), and they are becoming an increasingly larger percentage of the total damage costs from weather-related events at all scales and loss levels.
The U.S. losses from billion-dollar disasters over the last seven years (2015-2022) are more than $1 trillion and have further skewed the total distribution of extreme weather costs. From 1980-2000, about**75%**of all disaster-related costs were due to billion-dollar disasters, and by 2010, the percentage had risen to about**80%**. By 2022, it has risen to ~**85% of all disaster-related costs**, or $2.475 trillion out of $2.850 trillion.

## Increasing trend of high-cost disasters: exposure, vulnerability, and climate change
The number and cost of weather and climate disasters are increasing in the United States due to a combination of increasedexposure(i.e., more assets at risk),vulnerability(i.e., how much damage a hazard of given intensity—wind speed, or flood depth, for example—causes at a location), and the fact that climate change is increasing the frequency of some types of extremes that lead to billion-dollar disasters (NCA 2018, Chapter 2).
The history of billion-dollar disasters in the United States each year from 1980 to 2022, showing event type (colors), frequency (left-hand vertical axis), and cost (right-hand vertical axis.) The number and cost of weather and climate disasters is rising due to a combination of population growth and development along with the influence of human-caused climate change on some type of extreme events that lead to billion-dollar disasters. NOAA NCEI.
In other words, the increase in population and material wealth over the last several decades are an important cause for the rising costs. These trends are further complicated by the fact that much of the growth has taken place in vulnerable areas like coasts, the wildland-urban interface, and river floodplains. Vulnerability is especially high where building codes are insufficient for reducing damage from extreme events. This is part of the reason that the 2010s decade is far costlier than the 2000s, 1990s, or 1980s (all inflation adjusted to 2022 dollars).
Screenshot of a table of summary statistics of billion-dollar disasters by decade and by latest 1, 3-, and 5-year periods. NCEI Billion-dollar disaster web interface.
However, climate change is also supercharging theincreasing frequencyand intensity of certain types of extreme weather that lead to billion-dollar disasters—most notably the rise in vulnerability to drought, lengthening wildfire seasons in the Western states, and the potential for extremely heavy rainfall becoming more common in the eastern states. Sea level rise is worsening hurricanestorm surge flooding. (Read more about changes in climate and weather extremes in theU.S. National Climate Assessment.)Given all these compounding hazard risks, there is an increased need to focus on where we build, how we build, and investing in infrastructure updates that are designed for a 21 st-century climate.

## Notable U.S. billion-dollar disasters of 2022
### Hurricane Ian (September 2022): $112.9 billion, 152 deaths
Ian made landfall near Cayo Costa, Florida, as a Category 4 hurricane with sustained winds of 150 mph. Significant parts of coastal communities, including those along the barrier islands of Captiva, Sanibel, Pine and Fort Myers Beach, were swept away by the high winds and storm surge. Ian slowly crossed Florida causing significant inland flooding across central and eastern portions of the state from widespread rainfall totals of 10-20 inches. The counties of Volusia, Orange, Seminole and Brevard reported more than 20 inches of rainfall.
One of multiple washouts on the Sanibel Causeway near Fort Myers, Florida, following the passage of Hurricane Ian in 2022. Image captured September 29; provided by NOAA Remote Sensing Division.
Ian re-emerged over the Atlantic as a tropical storm, re-intensified into a Category 1 hurricane on September 30, and made landfall near Georgetown, SC, with sustained winds of 85 mph causing more coastal flood damage and destroying several large piers near Myrtle Beach, South Carolina. Since 1980, five hurricanes have produced $20+ billion in damage in Florida—Andrew (1992), Charley (2004), Wilma (2005), Irma (2017), and Michael (2018). Hurricanes Andrew and Irma produced the highest damage totals in Florida (approximately $50 billion for each storm). Hurricane Ian's impact is the first to exceed $100 billion in insured and uninsured losses in Florida.

## Notable U.S. billion-dollar disasters of 2022
### Western and Central Drought / Heat Wave (2022): $22.2 billion, 136 deaths
Lake Mead on August 17, 2022. Photo by Christopher Clark, Bureau of Reclamation. Used under Creative Commons license.
Severe drought conditions impacted the Western and Southern Plains states. Large reservoirs across the West including Lake Mead, Lake Powell, Lake Oroville, and Shasta Lake, among others, continue to be depleted. Lake Mead, the Nation's largest reservoir, is nearing dead pool status and is at the lowest level since it was filled in the 1930s. The Great Salt Lake is also near record-low levels. The impacts of the drought are affecting crops and feed costs for livestock. Extreme heat also developed for many days across Western and Central states causing more than one hundred heat-related fatalities across Arizona, Nevada, California, Oregon and Texas. This is one of the more costly droughts on record, with a diverse array of direct impacts across different regions and industries.

## 1980-2022 costs and fatalities by disaster type
The distribution of damage from U.S. billion-dollar disaster events from 1980 to 2022 is dominated by tropical cyclone losses. Tropical cyclones have caused the most damage ($1,333.6 billion) and have the highest average event cost ($22.2 billion per event). Drought ($327.7 billion), severe storms ($383.7 billion), and inland flooding ($177.9 billion) have also caused considerable damage based on the list of billion-dollar events.
Severe storms have caused the highest number of billion-dollar disaster events (163), but they have the lowest average event cost ($2.4 billion). Tropical cyclones and flooding represent the second and third most frequent event types (60 and 37), respectively. Tropical cyclones are responsible for the highest number of deaths (6,890), followed by drought/heatwave events (4,275) and severe storms (1,982).

## 2022 costs in historical context
In broader context, the total cost of U.S. billion-dollar disasters over the last 5 years (2018-2022) is**$595.5 billion**, with a 5-year annual cost average of**$119.1 billion**, the latter of which is nearly triple the 43-year inflation adjusted annual average cost. The U.S. billion-dollar disaster damage costs over the last 10-years (2013-2022) were also historically large: at least**$1.1 trillion**from 152 separate billion-dollar events.
It is important to keep in mind that these estimates do not reflect the total cost of U.S. weather and climate disasters, only those associated with events more than $1 billion in damages. That means they are a conservative estimate of how much extreme weather costs the United States each year. However, these billion-dollar events do account for most of the damage from all recorded U.S. weather and climate events (NCEI; Munich Re), and they are becoming an increasingly larger percentage of the total damage costs from weather-related events at all scales and loss levels.
The U.S. losses from billion-dollar disasters over the last seven years (2015-2022) are more than $1 trillion and have further skewed the total distribution of extreme weather costs. From 1980-2000, about**75%**of all disaster-related costs were due to billion-dollar disasters, and by 2010, the percentage had risen to about**80%**. By 2022, it has risen to ~**85% of all disaster-related costs**, or $2.475 trillion out of $2.850 trillion.

## Increasing trend of high-cost disasters: exposure, vulnerability, and climate change
The number and cost of weather and climate disasters are increasing in the United States due to a combination of increasedexposure(i.e., more assets at risk),vulnerability(i.e., how much damage a hazard of given intensity—wind speed, or flood depth, for example—causes at a location), and the fact that climate change is increasing the frequency of some types of extremes that lead to billion-dollar disasters (NCA 2018, Chapter 2).
The history of billion-dollar disasters in the United States each year from 1980 to 2022, showing event type (colors), frequency (left-hand vertical axis), and cost (right-hand vertical axis.) The number and cost of weather and climate disasters is rising due to a combination of population growth and development along with the influence of human-caused climate change on some type of extreme events that lead to billion-dollar disasters. NOAA NCEI.
In other words, the increase in population and material wealth over the last several decades are an important cause for the rising costs. These trends are further complicated by the fact that much of the growth has taken place in vulnerable areas like coasts, the wildland-urban interface, and river floodplains. Vulnerability is especially high where building codes are insufficient for reducing damage from extreme events. This is part of the reason that the 2010s decade is far costlier than the 2000s, 1990s, or 1980s (all inflation adjusted to 2022 dollars).
Screenshot of a table of summary statistics of billion-dollar disasters by decade and by latest 1, 3-, and 5-year periods. NCEI Billion-dollar disaster web interface.
However, climate change is also supercharging theincreasing frequencyand intensity of certain types of extreme weather that lead to billion-dollar disasters—most notably the rise in vulnerability to drought, lengthening wildfire seasons in the Western states, and the potential for extremely heavy rainfall becoming more common in the eastern states. Sea level rise is worsening hurricanestorm surge flooding. (Read more about changes in climate and weather extremes in theU.S. National Climate Assessment.)Given all these compounding hazard risks, there is an increased need to focus on where we build, how we build, and investing in infrastructure updates that are designed for a 21 st-century climate.

## Notable U.S. billion-dollar disasters of 2022
Among the many weather and climate-related disasters to affect the U.S. in 2022, the following caused the most damaging impacts and broke numerous records.

## Notable U.S. billion-dollar disasters of 2022
### Hurricane Ian (September 2022): $112.9 billion, 152 deaths
Ian made landfall near Cayo Costa, Florida, as a Category 4 hurricane with sustained winds of 150 mph. Significant parts of coastal communities, including those along the barrier islands of Captiva, Sanibel, Pine and Fort Myers Beach, were swept away by the high winds and storm surge. Ian slowly crossed Florida causing significant inland flooding across central and eastern portions of the state from widespread rainfall totals of 10-20 inches. The counties of Volusia, Orange, Seminole and Brevard reported more than 20 inches of rainfall.
One of multiple washouts on the Sanibel Causeway near Fort Myers, Florida, following the passage of Hurricane Ian in 2022. Image captured September 29; provided by NOAA Remote Sensing Division.
Ian re-emerged over the Atlantic as a tropical storm, re-intensified into a Category 1 hurricane on September 30, and made landfall near Georgetown, SC, with sustained winds of 85 mph causing more coastal flood damage and destroying several large piers near Myrtle Beach, South Carolina. Since 1980, five hurricanes have produced $20+ billion in damage in Florida—Andrew (1992), Charley (2004), Wilma (2005), Irma (2017), and Michael (2018). Hurricanes Andrew and Irma produced the highest damage totals in Florida (approximately $50 billion for each storm). Hurricane Ian's impact is the first to exceed $100 billion in insured and uninsured losses in Florida.

## Notable U.S. billion-dollar disasters of 2022
### Western and Central Drought / Heat Wave (2022): $22.2 billion, 136 deaths
Lake Mead on August 17, 2022. Photo by Christopher Clark, Bureau of Reclamation. Used under Creative Commons license.
Severe drought conditions impacted the Western and Southern Plains states. Large reservoirs across the West including Lake Mead, Lake Powell, Lake Oroville, and Shasta Lake, among others, continue to be depleted. Lake Mead, the Nation's largest reservoir, is nearing dead pool status and is at the lowest level since it was filled in the 1930s. The Great Salt Lake is also near record-low levels. The impacts of the drought are affecting crops and feed costs for livestock. Extreme heat also developed for many days across Western and Central states causing more than one hundred heat-related fatalities across Arizona, Nevada, California, Oregon and Texas. This is one of the more costly droughts on record, with a diverse array of direct impacts across different regions and industries.

## 1980-2022 costs and fatalities by disaster type
The distribution of damage from U.S. billion-dollar disaster events from 1980 to 2022 is dominated by tropical cyclone losses. Tropical cyclones have caused the most damage ($1,333.6 billion) and have the highest average event cost ($22.2 billion per event). Drought ($327.7 billion), severe storms ($383.7 billion), and inland flooding ($177.9 billion) have also caused considerable damage based on the list of billion-dollar events.
Severe storms have caused the highest number of billion-dollar disaster events (163), but they have the lowest average event cost ($2.4 billion). Tropical cyclones and flooding represent the second and third most frequent event types (60 and 37), respectively. Tropical cyclones are responsible for the highest number of deaths (6,890), followed by drought/heatwave events (4,275) and severe storms (1,982).

### Mid-season forecasts
Officially, the 2023 Atlantic hurricane season ran from June 1 to November 30.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-31) A total of 21 tropical cyclones formed, 20 of which intensified into nameable storms,[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-TWSAT_1123-32) ranking the season as the fourth-most active in terms of number of tropical or subtropical storms, tied with 1933.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-EOTS_1130-27) Of those, seven strengthened into a hurricane, with three systems reaching major hurricane intensity. Thus, the season was above-average compared to NOAA's 1991–2020 mean of fourteen named storms, while equaling the normal number of hurricanes and major hurricanes, seven and three, respectively.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-TWSAT_1123-32) NOAA attributed the abnormally high number of named storms to record-warm sea surface temperatures across the Atlantic, mostly offsetting the effects of a strong El Niño event, which typically limits activity in the basin.

### Mid-season forecasts
In fact, the season had the most tropical or subtropical storms for a year with El Niño conditions present since records began.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-NOAA_Summary-33) Meteorologists such as Jonathan Belles and Phil Klotzbach argued that El Niño impacted the season by significantly weakening and shifting the Bermuda high-pressure system eastward, causing several storms to recurve out to sea much farther east than usual or drift aimlessly over the central Atlantic, rather than being pushed westward towards the continental United States, Mexico, or Central America.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Post_2211-34)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-35) Consequently, only three systems made landfall in the United States.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-HURDAT-36)

### Mid-season forecasts
Few tropical cyclones in the Atlantic in 2023 left significant impacts. The most destructive storm, Idalia, caused 12 deaths and approximately $3.6 billion in damage in August despite making landfall in Florida at Category 3 hurricane intensity, due to crossing mostly rural areas.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-itcr-37) During the same month, Franklin rendered at least $90 million in damage and three deaths, all in the Dominican Republic, which it struck as a weak tropical storm.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-ftcr-38) Although Lee remained offshore while a tropical cyclone, rough seas generated by the storm drowned four people, while the remnants resulted in about $50 million in damage, mostly in Maine and Atlantic Canada.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-ltcr-39) In September, Ophelia caused approximately $450 million in damage along the East Coast of the United States.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-otcr-40) Overall, the storms of the 2023 season collectively inflicted more than $4.22 billion in damage and 19 fatalities.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-41)

### Mid-season forecasts
This season's ACE index was approximately 148.2 units,[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-ACE-42) roughly 21% above average.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-43) This number represents sum of the squares of the maximum sustained wind speed (knots) for all named storms while they are at least tropical storm intensity, divided by 10,000. Therefore, tropical depressions are not included.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Background-6)
In 2023, NOAA logged 468 flight hours for their Hurricane Hunter missions in the Atlantic. The aircraft deployed more than 1,400 scientific instruments and conducted 120 entries into the eye of a storm. NOAA launched several drones, including Black Swift drone for the first time into Tammy, both for obtaining observations and evaluating the efficiency of this method of collecting data. Additionally, NOAA used their aircraft to assist with emergency response to Idalia and Lee, conducting a combined 28 flight hours to obtain aerial imagery. The National Ocean Service, an agency of NOAA, surveyed just over 42 mi (68 km) of coastline, including identifying 29 potential marine obstructions, in the aftermath of Idalia.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-NOAA_Summary-33)

### Mid-season forecasts
The 2023 Atlantic hurricane season commenced unexpectedly on January 16, when an unnamed subtropical storm formed off the northeastern U.S. coast then moved over Atlantic Canada.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Unnamed_TCR-44) Operationally, the NHC considered the storm to be non-tropical, with minimal likelihood of transitioning into a subtropical or tropical cyclone.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-January_ss-45) A few months later, however, following a post-storm evaluation of the system, it was redesignated as subtropical, but intentionally left unnamed.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Unnamed_TCR-44)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-46) No additional tropical or subtropical activity occurred in the basin prior to the official start of the season on June 1. Tropical Depression Two formed on opening day in the Gulf of Mexico.

### Mid-season forecasts
It became the season's first named storm, Arlene, on June 2.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Arlene_TCR-47) Later that month, tropical storms Bret and Cindy formed, becoming the first instance of two Atlantic tropical cyclones active simultaneously in June since 1968.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-48) The two developed in the Main Development Region (MDR) from successive tropical waves coming off the coast of West Africa.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-MastersClimate-49) Their formation also marked the first time on record that two tropical storms formed in the MDR during the month of June.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-JuneMDR-50) Next, Subtropical Storm Don formed over the central Atlantic on July 14. A long-lived storm, it later became fully tropical and strengthened into the season's first hurricane as it meandered around the ocean far from land.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-51)

### Tropical Storm Harold
On August 23, a trough of low pressure formed in the Eastern Pacific basin offshore of the Central America coast. The disturbance crossed over into the Atlantic basin and began to organize as it moved northward through the northwestern Caribbean, where a low-pressure area formed on August 25. The pace of organization quickened on August 26, with a tropical depression developing at 12:00 UTC about 45 mi (70 km) east-southeast of Cancún, Mexico. Later that day, and into the next, the depression drifted due to weak surrounding steering currents, with its center moving in a small counter-clockwise loop. A brief jog southward moved the depression over Cancún around 06:00 UTC on August 27. About six hours later, the cyclone intensified into Tropical Storm Idalia. Early on August 28, Idalia began moving northward toward the Yucatán Channel west of Cuba, intensifying along the way. After passing near the western tip of Cuba early the next day, the storm strengthened into a hurricane.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-itcr-37)

### Tropical Storm Harold
Due to warm sea surface temperatures, low wind shear, and moist air, Idalia rapidly intensified as it accelerated northward through the Gulf of Mexico, reaching Category 4 strength early on August 30 and peaking with maximum sustained winds of 130 mph (215 km/h) and a minimum central pressure of 942 mbar (27.82 inHg).[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-itcr-37) Idalia's strengthening was then halted by an eyewall replacement cycle, which caused it to weaken slightly before it made landfall at 11:45 UTC, near Keaton Beach, Florida, with sustained winds of 115 mph (185 km/h).[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-itcr-37)[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-121) Idalia quickly weakened as it moved inland into southeast Georgia, and it was downgraded to a tropical storm at 18:00 UTC that same day. Strong southwesterly wind shear then pushed the storm's convection well north and east of its center as it moved off the northeastern South Carolina coast and emerged into the Atlantic early on August 31. Around 12:00 UTC, while about 60 mi (95 km) east of Cape Fear, North Carolina, Idalia transitioned into an extratropical cyclone.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-itcr-37) The storm then moved slowly eastward and impacted Bermuda with tropical-storm-force winds on September 2, as it passed just to the south.

### Tropical Storm Harold
Idalia's remnant low then absorbed Tropical Storm Gert,[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Zelinsky-101) turned northward, and lingered offshore Atlantic Canada for several days before dissipating on September 8.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-itcr-37)

### Tropical Storm Harold
During the storm's early stages, heavy rains fell along the Yucatán Peninsula and in western Cuba.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-122) Consequently, flooding occurred in some areas of the latter, especially in Artemisa and Pinar del Río provinces, forcing the evacuation of over 10,000 people. In Florida, high winds and storm surge reaching up to 8 to 12 ft (2.4 to 3.7 m) above the ground between Keaton Beach and Steinhatchee caused significant damage across the Big Bend region of Florida to agriculture, infrastructure, and buildings and residences, which were flooded up to several miles inland.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-itcr-37) Severe storm surge impacts extended southward to parts of the Tampa Bay area, with up to 5 ft (1.5 m) of water reported in approximately 2,000 homes in Pasco County. Roughly 150 people in the county required rescue during the storm.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-123) Tens of thousands of structures in Florida outside the Big Bend region sustained some degree of damage. Parts of Georgia and the Carolinas experienced rains, strong winds, storm surge, and tornadoes, but with lesser impacts than in Florida, while high tides were reported as far north as the Mid-Atlantic. Overall, Idalia caused approximately $3.6 billion in damage and twelve deaths in the United States – four in Florida, three each in North Carolina and New Jersey, and one each in Georgia and Delaware.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-itcr-37) The remnants of Idalia caused more than 6,000 power outages on Bermuda and the delay or cancellation of many flights to and from the L.F. Wade International Airport.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-124)

### Tropical Storm Jose

On August 19, a vigorous tropical wave moved off the west coast of Africa. After traversing the Cabo Verde Islands, a low-pressure area developed on August 24.

### Tropical Storm Jose
The disturbance struggled to organize until August 29,[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-jtcr-125) when persistent deep convection reignited over the eastern side of the circulation.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-126) Consequently, Tropical Depression Eleven formed about 850 mi (1,370 km) southeast of Bermuda.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-jtcr-125) The depression meandered due weak steering currents over the next two days, and by August 30, had become less organized due to westerly shear.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-127) However, the shear briefly relaxed, and the storm's convective bursting pattern abruptly evolved into curved banding early on August 31, signifying that the depression had strengthened into Tropical Storm Jose.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-jtcr-125)[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-128) Further development occurred slowly as Jose's banding features remained limited, and the convection at its center was shallow.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-129) Even so, the storm's structure improved markedly early on September 1 as convection near the center deepened and a small mid-level eye feature appeared, causing Jose to peak with maximum sustained winds of 65 mph (100 km/h).[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-jtcr-125) This intensification was short lived however,

### Tropical Storm Katia
On September 1, a tropical wave emerged into the tropical Atlantic from the west coast of Africa.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-ltcr-39) A broad surface low formed by September 4, which acquired multiple low-level bands developing and a well-defined center on the next day.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-ltcr-39)[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-133) Consequently, Tropical Depression Thirteen developed at 12:00 UTC that day about halfway between the west coast of Africa and the Lesser Antilles. Amid favorable conditions for intensification, the depression quickly strengthened into Tropical Storm Lee six hours later and a then a hurricane by late on September 6. Then, during the 24‑hour period ending at 06:00 UTC on September 8, Lee experienced explosive intensification, and reached Category 5 strength, with its winds increasing by 80 mph (130 km/h) to 165 mph (270 km/h).[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-ltcr-39) However, increasing southwesterly wind shear quickly caused Lee's eye to become cloud filled and the storm became more asymmetric, weakening it back to a high-end Category 4 hurricane.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-134) The pace of weakening quickened as the day progressed, and Lee fell below major hurricane status by late on September 9,[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-ltcr-39) according to data from an evening hurricane hunters mission revealing that the storm was undergoing an eyewall replacement cycle and still being adversely affected by wind shear.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-135)

### Tropical Storm Katia
By September 10, wind shear abated, permitting the new, larger-diameter eye to contract and to grow more symmetric.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-136) As a result, Lee intensified to Category 3 strength once again that same day. Another series of eyewall replacement cycles led to fluctuations in its size and intensity, but Lee remained a major hurricane throughout. After tracking west-northwestward to northwestward for much of its trans‑Atlantic journey, Lee turned northward on September 13, moving around the western side of the steering subtropical ridge. That same day, it also weakened to Category 2 strength.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-ltcr-39) Then, on the morning of September 14, Lee became a Category 1 hurricane while approaching Bermuda,[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-137) which it passed to the west by 185 mi (300 km) later in the day.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-138) As the hurricane pushed northward, continued drier air entrainment and increasingly strong southerly wind shear displaced Lee's convection to the northern side of the system, weakening it further. These factors caused the hurricane to commence its extratropical transition,[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-139) which was completed by 06:00 UTC on September 16. Later that day and throughout the next two days, the extratropical cyclone made several landfalls in Atlantic Canada before moving into the northern Atlantic and merging with another extratropical low late on September 18.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-ltcr-39)

### Tropical Storm Katia
Rip currents caused one fatality in Puerto Rico when a 66-year-old man drowned at Poza del Obispo. Additionally, Lee generated dangerous surf and rip currents along the entire Atlantic coast of the United States. Lee produced hurricane-force winds gusts, along with flooding rains, mostly in Maine and Atlantic Canada. Consequently, approximately 200,000 power outages occurred in the United States, mostly in Maine, and a similar number in the Canadian provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. Maine and Atlantic Canada also reported many downed trees and power lines, as well as flash flooding, leading to road closures. ### Mid-season forecasts
Officially, the 2023 Atlantic hurricane season ran from June 1 to November 30.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-31) A total of 21 tropical cyclones formed, 20 of which intensified into nameable storms,[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-TWSAT_1123-32) ranking the season as the fourth-most active in terms of number of tropical or subtropical storms, tied with 1933.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-EOTS_1130-27) Of those, seven strengthened into a hurricane, with three systems reaching major hurricane intensity. Thus, the season was above-average compared to NOAA's 1991–2020 mean of fourteen named storms, while equaling the normal number of hurricanes and major hurricanes, seven and three, respectively.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-TWSAT_1123-32) NOAA attributed the abnormally high number of named storms to record-warm sea surface temperatures across the Atlantic, mostly offsetting the effects of a strong El Niño event, which typically limits activity in the basin.
texts.13:
### Mid-season forecasts
In fact, the season had the most tropical or subtropical storms for a year with El Niño conditions present since records began.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-NOAA_Summary-33) Meteorologists such as Jonathan Belles and Phil Klotzbach argued that El Niño impacted the season by significantly weakening and shifting the Bermuda high-pressure system eastward, causing several storms to recurve out to sea much farther east than usual or drift aimlessly over the central Atlantic, rather than being pushed westward towards the continental United States, Mexico, or Central America.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Post_2211-34)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-35) Consequently, only three systems made landfall in the United States.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-HURDAT-36)

### Mid-season forecasts
Few tropical cyclones in the Atlantic in 2023 left significant impacts. The most destructive storm, Idalia, caused 12 deaths and approximately $3.6 billion in damage in August despite making landfall in Florida at Category 3 hurricane intensity, due to crossing mostly rural areas.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-itcr-37) During the same month, Franklin rendered at least $90 million in damage and three deaths, all in the Dominican Republic, which it struck as a weak tropical storm.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-ftcr-38) Although Lee remained offshore while a tropical cyclone, rough seas generated by the storm drowned four people, while the remnants resulted in about $50 million in damage, mostly in Maine and Atlantic Canada.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-ltcr-39) In September, Ophelia caused approximately $450 million in damage along the East Coast of the United States.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-otcr-40) Overall, the storms of the 2023 season collectively inflicted more than $4.22 billion in damage and 19 fatalities.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-41)

### Mid-season forecasts
This season's ACE index was approximately 148.2 units,[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-ACE-42) roughly 21% above average.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-43) This number represents sum of the squares of the maximum sustained wind speed (knots) for all named storms while they are at least tropical storm intensity, divided by 10,000. Therefore, tropical depressions are not included.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Background-6)
In 2023, NOAA logged 468 flight hours for their Hurricane Hunter missions in the Atlantic. The aircraft deployed more than 1,400 scientific instruments and conducted 120 entries into the eye of a storm. NOAA launched several drones, including Black Swift drone for the first time into Tammy, both for obtaining observations and evaluating the efficiency of this method of collecting data. Additionally, NOAA used their aircraft to assist with emergency response to Idalia and Lee, conducting a combined 28 flight hours to obtain aerial imagery. The National Ocean Service, an agency of NOAA, surveyed just over 42 mi (68 km) of coastline, including identifying 29 potential marine obstructions, in the aftermath of Idalia.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-NOAA_Summary-33)

### Mid-season forecasts
The 2023 Atlantic hurricane season commenced unexpectedly on January 16, when an unnamed subtropical storm formed off the northeastern U.S. coast then moved over Atlantic Canada.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Unnamed_TCR-44) Operationally, the NHC considered the storm to be non-tropical, with minimal likelihood of transitioning into a subtropical or tropical cyclone.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-January_ss-45) A few months later, however, following a post-storm evaluation of the system, it was redesignated as subtropical, but intentionally left unnamed.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Unnamed_TCR-44)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-46) No additional tropical or subtropical activity occurred in the basin prior to the official start of the season on June 1. Tropical Depression Two formed on opening day in the Gulf of Mexico.

### Mid-season forecasts
It became the season's first named storm, Arlene, on June 2.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Arlene_TCR-47) Later that month, tropical storms Bret and Cindy formed, becoming the first instance of two Atlantic tropical cyclones active simultaneously in June since 1968.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-48) The two developed in the Main Development Region (MDR) from successive tropical waves coming off the coast of West Africa.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-MastersClimate-49) Their formation also marked the first time on record that two tropical storms formed in the MDR during the month of June.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-JuneMDR-50) Next, Subtropical Storm Don formed over the central Atlantic on July 14. A long-lived storm, it later became fully tropical and strengthened into the season's first hurricane as it meandered around the ocean far from land.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-51)
texts.44:
### Tropical Storm Harold
On August 23, a trough of low pressure formed in the Eastern Pacific basin offshore of the Central America coast. The disturbance crossed over into the Atlantic basin and began to organize as it moved northward through the northwestern Caribbean, where a low-pressure area formed on August 25. The pace of organization quickened on August 26, with a tropical depression developing at 12:00 UTC about 45 mi (70 km) east-southeast of Cancún, Mexico. Later that day, and into the next, the depression drifted due to weak surrounding steering currents, with its center moving in a small counter-clockwise loop. A brief jog southward moved the depression over Cancún around 06:00 UTC on August 27. About six hours later, the cyclone intensified into Tropical Storm Idalia. Early on August 28, Idalia began moving northward toward the Yucatán Channel west of Cuba, intensifying along the way. After passing near the western tip of Cuba early the next day, the storm strengthened into a hurricane.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-itcr-37)
texts.45:
### Tropical Storm Harold
Due to warm sea surface temperatures, low wind shear, and moist air, Idalia rapidly intensified as it accelerated northward through the Gulf of Mexico, reaching Category 4 strength early on August 30 and peaking with maximum sustained winds of 130 mph (215 km/h) and a minimum central pressure of 942 mbar (27.82 inHg).[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-itcr-37) Idalia's strengthening was then halted by an eyewall replacement cycle, which caused it to weaken slightly before it made landfall at 11:45 UTC, near Keaton Beach, Florida, with sustained winds of 115 mph (185 km/h).[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-itcr-37)[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-121) Idalia quickly weakened as it moved inland into southeast Georgia, and it was downgraded to a tropical storm at 18:00 UTC that same day. Strong southwesterly wind shear then pushed the storm's convection well north and east of its center as it moved off the northeastern South Carolina coast and emerged into the Atlantic early on August 31. Around 12:00 UTC, while about 60 mi (95 km) east of Cape Fear, North Carolina, Idalia transitioned into an extratropical cyclone.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-itcr-37) The storm then moved slowly eastward and impacted Bermuda with tropical-storm-force winds on September 2, as it passed just to the south.

### Tropical Storm Harold
Idalia's remnant low then absorbed Tropical Storm Gert,[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Zelinsky-101) turned northward, and lingered offshore Atlantic Canada for several days before dissipating on September 8.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-itcr-37)

### Tropical Storm Harold
During the storm's early stages, heavy rains fell along the Yucatán Peninsula and in western Cuba.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-122) Consequently, flooding occurred in some areas of the latter, especially in Artemisa and Pinar del Río provinces, forcing the evacuation of over 10,000 people. In Florida, high winds and storm surge reaching up to 8 to 12 ft (2.4 to 3.7 m) above the ground between Keaton Beach and Steinhatchee caused significant damage across the Big Bend region of Florida to agriculture, infrastructure, and buildings and residences, which were flooded up to several miles inland.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-itcr-37) Severe storm surge impacts extended southward to parts of the Tampa Bay area, with up to 5 ft (1.5 m) of water reported in approximately 2,000 homes in Pasco County. Roughly 150 people in the county required rescue during the storm.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-123) Tens of thousands of structures in Florida outside the Big Bend region sustained some degree of damage. Parts of Georgia and the Carolinas experienced rains, strong winds, storm surge, and tornadoes, but with lesser impacts than in Florida, while high tides were reported as far north as the Mid-Atlantic. Overall, Idalia caused approximately $3.6 billion in damage and twelve deaths in the United States – four in Florida, three each in North Carolina and New Jersey, and one each in Georgia and Delaware.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-itcr-37) The remnants of Idalia caused more than 6,000 power outages on Bermuda and the delay or cancellation of many flights to and from the L.F. Wade International Airport.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-124)

### Tropical Storm Jose
The disturbance struggled to organize until August 29,[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-jtcr-125) when persistent deep convection reignited over the eastern side of the circulation.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-126) Consequently, Tropical Depression Eleven formed about 850 mi (1,370 km) southeast of Bermuda.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-jtcr-125) The depression meandered due weak steering currents over the next two days, and by August 30, had become less organized due to westerly shear.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-127) However, the shear briefly relaxed, and the storm's convective bursting pattern abruptly evolved into curved banding early on August 31, signifying that the depression had strengthened into Tropical Storm Jose.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-jtcr-125)[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-128) Further development occurred slowly as Jose's banding features remained limited, and the convection at its center was shallow.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-129) Even so, the storm's structure improved markedly early on September 1 as convection near the center deepened and a small mid-level eye feature appeared, causing Jose to peak with maximum sustained winds of 65 mph (100 km/h).[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-jtcr-125) This intensification was short lived however,

### Tropical Storm Katia
On September 1, a tropical wave emerged into the tropical Atlantic from the west coast of Africa.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-ltcr-39) A broad surface low formed by September 4, which acquired multiple low-level bands developing and a well-defined center on the next day.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-ltcr-39)[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-133) Consequently, Tropical Depression Thirteen developed at 12:00 UTC that day about halfway between the west coast of Africa and the Lesser Antilles. Amid favorable conditions for intensification, the depression quickly strengthened into Tropical Storm Lee six hours later and a then a hurricane by late on September 6. Then, during the 24‑hour period ending at 06:00 UTC on September 8, Lee experienced explosive intensification, and reached Category 5 strength, with its winds increasing by 80 mph (130 km/h) to 165 mph (270 km/h).[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-ltcr-39) However, increasing southwesterly wind shear quickly caused Lee's eye to become cloud filled and the storm became more asymmetric, weakening it back to a high-end Category 4 hurricane.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-134) The pace of weakening quickened as the day progressed, and Lee fell below major hurricane status by late on September 9,[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-ltcr-39) according to data from an evening hurricane hunters mission revealing that the storm was undergoing an eyewall replacement cycle and still being adversely affected by wind shear.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-135)

By September 10, wind shear abated, permitting the new, larger-diameter eye to contract and to grow more symmetric.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-136) As a result, Lee intensified to Category 3 strength once again that same day. These factors caused the hurricane to commence its extratropical transition,[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-139) which was completed by 06:00 UTC on September 16. Later that day and throughout the next two days, the extratropical cyclone made several landfalls in Atlantic Canada before moving into the northern Atlantic and merging with another extratropical low late on September 18.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-ltcr-39)
